section_summary: This section records U.S. discussions with SCAP and the Far Eastern Commission over Japanese fishing areas and Antarctic whaling in 1947. Officials weigh Japan’s food needs against Allied objections and international whaling limits, then examine reports that the 1946–47 expedition wasted whale products and breached whaling rules. The section ends with the beginning of a study of Japan’s four largest fishing companies.

subfiles.title: Policy with respect to Japanese fishing
subfiles.to: Informal Interagency Committee on Japanese Fishing and Marine Industry
subfiles.about: The committee discusses Allied pressure to restrict Japanese fishing and whaling.
subfiles.summary: Reporting a February 11 meeting, the memorandum contrasts a restrictive Allied approach with U.S. support for Japanese economic recovery. Members consider a compromise on whaling, fishing boundaries, vessel size and SCAP discretion, and call for further consultation.

subfiles.title: Note on Japanese fisheries studies
subfiles.about: A handwritten note records the status or classification of Japanese fisheries studies.
subfiles.summary: The partially illegible note appears to say the studies are unfinished and unavailable.

subfiles.title: Request for Japanese fisheries study reports
subfiles.about: Siam requests copies of Allied studies of Japanese fisheries.
subfiles.summary: The Siamese Legation seeks study documents and reports for its Department of Fisheries.

subfiles.title: Reply concerning Japanese fisheries studies
subfiles.about: The State Department replies to Siam’s request for study reports.
subfiles.summary: The reply says the studies are incomplete and offers to provide reports when available.

subfiles.title: Antarctic whaling catch statistics, February 2–8
subfiles.about: SCAP reports weekly Japanese Antarctic blue whale catches.
subfiles.summary: Hashidate Maru caught 39½ blue whale units and Nissin Maru 49½.

subfiles.title: Antarctic whaling catch statistics, February 9–15
subfiles.about: Tokyo reports weekly blue whale catches by Japanese factory ships.
subfiles.summary: The telegram supplies catches for Hashidate Maru and Nissin Maru; the first figure is illegible.

subfiles.title: Policy with respect to Japanese fishing
subfiles.about: The committee agrees on a possible compromise for Far Eastern Commission discussions.
subfiles.summary: Members favor retaining FEC-035 while requiring Far Eastern Commission consultation and approval for whaling outside the SCAPIN 1033 area.

subfiles.title: Antarctic whaling catch statistics, February 16–22
subfiles.about: SCAP reports another week of Japanese Antarctic catches.
subfiles.summary: Hashidate Maru caught 35 blue whale units and Nissin Maru 40.

subfiles.title: Japanese fishing policy
subfiles.about: Bowman reports an Australian suggestion for consultation before expanding Japanese fishing waters.
subfiles.summary: Major Plimsoll suggests that SCAP consult the Allied Council before further extensions.

subfiles.title: Japanese fishing areas and food needs
subfiles.about: Tokyo urges that policy leave room to expand Japan’s fishing areas.
subfiles.summary: Whitman cites protein shortages, proposed operations near China and Kamchatka, and the importance of fishing near Midway and mandated islands.

subfiles.title: Japanese fishing areas: proposed cable to SCAP
subfiles.about: Martin proposes instructions seeking SCAP’s response to a fishing and whaling compromise.
subfiles.summary: The draft would preserve SCAP control over fishing areas while requiring FEC approval for whaling outside the existing area. It proposes Allied Council consultation on substantial area extensions, except those made through bilateral agreements.

subfiles.title: Antarctic whaling catch statistics, February 23–March 8
subfiles.about: Tokyo reports catches and the end of Hashidate Maru’s operations.
subfiles.summary: The telegram gives two weeks of catches and says Hashidate Maru ceased operations February 25.

subfiles.title: Japanese fishing areas
subfiles.about: An official recommends approval of the proposed cable to SCAP.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum explains the FEC compromise and notes War Department concurrence.

subfiles.title: Japanese fishing areas routing note
subfiles.about: A brief, mostly illegible note concerns handling the fishing areas cable.
subfiles.summary: The note appears to record clearance or transmission arrangements.

subfiles.title: Cable on Japanese fishing areas
subfiles.about: The cable sets out the proposed FEC compromise on fishing areas and whaling.
subfiles.summary: It seeks to retain SCAP’s discretion over fishing boundaries while requiring approval for whaling beyond the SCAPIN 1033 area.

subfiles.title: Transmission of cable on a second Antarctic expedition
subfiles.about: A proposed telegram explains opposition to a second Japanese Antarctic whaling expedition.
subfiles.summary: The draft weighs Japan’s need for food and oil against firm British, Australian and New Zealand objections, the conventional catch limit, and conservation commitments. It proposes refusing the expedition while defending Japan’s longer-term right to whaling.

subfiles.title: Proposed Japanese Antarctic whaling expedition, 1947–48
subfiles.about: Allison recommends against authorizing a second SCAP expedition.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum examines legal, diplomatic and conservation risks, along with the expedition’s expected economic value. Allison concludes that the United States should refuse authorization and seek whale meat and oil for Japan from Allied catches.

subfiles.title: SCAP’s 1947–48 whaling expedition
subfiles.about: The memorandum forwards an interim draft cable while a final decision is prepared.
subfiles.summary: It notes likely refusal of the expedition and a need for consultation.

subfiles.title: Interim cable on a second Antarctic whaling expedition
subfiles.about: The draft asks SCAP to await a U.S. decision on a second expedition.
subfiles.summary: It relays Allied objections and says State is considering their implications. If authorization is refused, State proposes seeking replacement products from Allied catches.

subfiles.title: Whaling
subfiles.about: Fearey opposes the proposed expedition over concern for whaling agreements.
subfiles.summary: Fearey suggests asking Allied whalers to replace Japan’s previous catch.

subfiles.title: Proposed Japanese Antarctic whaling expedition
subfiles.about: Hickerson recommends against another Japanese Antarctic expedition.
subfiles.summary: He argues that the expedition would shift catches and foreign exchange from Allied whalers to Japan and damage U.S. relations with interested governments.

subfiles.title: 1947–48 Japanese Antarctic whaling expedition
subfiles.about: Hilldring consults Allied representatives on a proposed SCAP expedition.
subfiles.summary: Hilldring presents U.S. arguments based on Japan’s food needs and occupation costs. British, Australian, New Zealand and Norwegian representatives reiterate objections involving the catch limit, conservation, competition and relations with the United States. Hilldring promises further consultation before a final decision.

subfiles.title: Australian observer’s report on whaling expedition
subfiles.about: Fearey assesses reported waste aboard a Japanese whaling vessel.
subfiles.summary: He urges SCAP to examine apparent violations and prevent their recurrence.

subfiles.title: Request for clearance of whaling cable
subfiles.about: A cover memorandum requests concurrence in a draft cable on whaling rules.
subfiles.summary: It forwards a State-originated draft listing applicable international whaling provisions.

subfiles.title: Whaling rules applicable to the 1947–48 season
subfiles.about: The draft lists applicable whaling agreements and warns against waste.
subfiles.summary: It outlines convention provisions for the coming season and raises concern that poor equipment and discarded oil-bearing material caused losses in 1946–47. It tells SCAP to limit catches to whales that can be properly processed.

subfiles.title: Routing slip for whaling cable
subfiles.about: A routing slip requests comment or concurrence on the cable.
subfiles.summary: The slip bears a brief handwritten clearance request.

subfiles.title: Dispatch of cable and aide-memoire regarding Antarctic whaling
subfiles.about: Fearey seeks clearance of a strong cable on violations of whaling rules.
subfiles.summary: He cites the Australian observer, SCAP comments and Kellogg’s expert report.

subfiles.title: Draft telegram on whale-product waste
subfiles.about: The draft challenges discarding oil-bearing whale material.
subfiles.summary: It calls for equipment repairs and catches limited to processing capacity.

subfiles.title: Revised draft telegram on whaling violations
subfiles.about: A revised draft asks SCAP about breaches of whaling regulations.
subfiles.summary: It challenges the authorization of discarded bones, asks about action over undersized whales, and urges strict compliance in 1947–48.

subfiles.title: Further draft telegram on whaling violations
subfiles.about: Another draft repeats questions about waste and enforcement.
subfiles.summary: It cites discarded oil-bearing material, low oil yield and undersized whales, and calls for corrective measures before the next expedition.

subfiles.title: Comments on despatch 1188 and the Australian observer’s report
subfiles.about: The International Resources Division evaluates alleged violations during 1946–47 whaling.
subfiles.summary: Drawing on Kellogg’s assessment and the 1937 London Agreement, Flory concludes that discarding bones violated processing rules and contributed to low oil output. He asks whether infractions and the taking of undersized whales were investigated and punished. The division may withdraw support for future expeditions unless SCAP acts.

subfiles.title: Draft telegram to SCAP
subfiles.about: Castleman forwards a reference outline of whaling rules for SCAP.
subfiles.summary: He requests transmission and promises the full provisions by airmail.

subfiles.title: International whaling provisions for 1947–48
subfiles.about: The draft identifies treaty and protocol provisions applicable to the season.
subfiles.summary: It lists rules on species, seasons, factory ships, processing, enforcement, remuneration and statistics.

subfiles.title: Final Antarctic whaling catch statistics
subfiles.about: Tokyo reports the final catch and close of the expedition.
subfiles.summary: Nissin Maru caught 29½ units March 9–15; all activities then ceased.

subfiles.title: Japanese fishing near Soviet-controlled areas
subfiles.about: SCAP prepares a plan for Japanese fishing near Kamchatka.
subfiles.summary: Atcheson recommends considering Soviet acceptance of minimum operations, while noting possible implications for Alaska, the Aleutians and FEC negotiations.

subfiles.title: Statistics supplied to the International Bureau for Whaling Statistics
subfiles.about: Tokyo forwards vessel and crew details sent to Sandefjord.
subfiles.summary: The airgram lists factory ships, catchers and Japanese crews.

subfiles.title: SCAP views on fishing compromise and further whaling
subfiles.about: SCAP responds to the proposed FEC compromise and argues for another expedition.
subfiles.summary: SCAP accepts consultation over substantial fishing-area extensions but disputes Allied objections to emergency Antarctic whaling. The telegram stresses Japan’s food and oil needs and asks for replacement supplies if whaling is barred.

subfiles.title: Preliminary study of large Japanese fishing companies
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: The Political Adviser forwards copies of a study of major fishing companies.
subfiles.summary: Despatch 939 transmits Natural Resources Section Preliminary Study No. 5.

subfiles.title: Japan’s Big Fishing Companies
subfiles.from: John L. Kask, Natural Resources Section, SCAP
subfiles.about: The study profiles Japan’s four largest prewar fishing and whaling companies.
subfiles.summary: The study identifies Nippon Suisan, Nichiro Gyogyo, Taiyo Gyogyo and Kyokuyo Hogei as dominant firms and describes their production, fleets, ownership and wartime losses. Its opening detailed section traces Nippon Suisan’s mergers, reorganization, shareholders and overseas subsidiaries in Argentina, Taiwan, Borneo, the Philippines, Manchuria, Korea and China. The study continues beyond page 382.
